youtube.title: Nile Dam (GERD): Egypt, Ethiopia and the River Deal Never Signed
youtube.description:
On the Blue Nile, close to the Sudan border, a reservoir now holds up to 74 billion cubic metres of water. Downstream, Egypt says the Nile gives it about 97 percent of its water. Ethiopia finished Africa's largest hydroelectric dam in 2025. So why do the two countries still have no agreement on how to run it?

We follow the river on the map: where the water really comes from, the treaties of 1902, 1929 and 1959 that divided it, the 2015 declaration that left the key numbers blank, each side's case in its strongest form, and three scenarios, from a binding deal to a long drought, that could redraw the Nile.

{CHAPTERS}

youtube.comment: Should a river's water be shared by where it falls as rain, or by who has used it longest? 👇

sources.claim: The GERD reservoir can hold 74 billion cubic metres of water
sources.source: Ethiopian Electric Power, project data; Reuters, 9 Sept 2025

sources.claim: GERD is Africa's largest hydroelectric dam
sources.source: Reuters and AP reporting on the inauguration, 9 Sept 2025

sources.claim: Ethiopia formally inaugurated the dam in September 2025
sources.source: Reuters, AP, 9 Sept 2025

sources.claim: Construction took fourteen years; foundation stone laid in April 2011
sources.source: Ethiopian government, foundation ceremony 2 April 2011; Reuters, 9 Sept 2025

sources.claim: Egypt says the Nile supplies about 97 percent of its water
sources.source: Egyptian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, statements to the UN Security Council, 29 June 2020 and 8 July 2021

sources.claim: Egypt is one of the world's largest wheat importers
sources.source: USDA Foreign Agricultural Service, Grain: World Markets and Trade, 2024/25

sources.claim: Anglo-Ethiopian Treaty signed May 1902, Article III on the Blue Nile, Lake Tana and the Sobat
sources.source: Treaty between the United Kingdom and Ethiopia, Addis Ababa, 15 May 1902 (British and Foreign State Papers)

sources.claim: The Nile runs about 6,650 km through a basin shared by eleven countries
sources.source: Nile Basin Initiative, State of the River Nile Basin report, 2012/2021

sources.claim: The Blue Nile supplies about 59 percent of the flow at Aswan; with the Atbara and Sobat, roughly 85 percent comes from Ethiopia; studies differ by a few points
sources.source: Sutcliffe and Parks, The Hydrology of the Nile (IAHS, 1999); Nile Basin Initiative, 2012

sources.claim: Most Blue Nile flow comes in the June–September rainy season
sources.source: Sutcliffe and Parks, The Hydrology of the Nile, 1999

sources.claim: GERD's main dam is 145 m high and about 1.8 km long
sources.source: Ethiopian Electric Power, project specification; Webuild (main contractor) project page

sources.claim: Average Nile flow at Aswan is about 84 billion cubic metres a year
sources.source: Agreement between Egypt and Sudan for the Full Utilization of the Nile Waters, 8 Nov 1959

sources.claim: GERD is rated at 5,150 MW; Aswan High Dam at 2,100 MW
sources.source: Ethiopian Electric Power, 2025; Egyptian Electricity Holding Company, annual report

sources.claim: Ethiopia has more than 120 million people; about 45 percent had no electricity in 2022
sources.source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (population; access to electricity 55%, 2022)

sources.claim: Roseires Dam is about 100 km downstream of GERD in a straight line
sources.source: Our measurement between published dam coordinates (GERD 11.215N 35.093E; Roseires 11.80N 34.39E)

sources.claim: In July 2020 Sudan's irrigation ministry reported a sharp drop in the river and linked it to GERD's filling
sources.source: Sudan Ministry of Irrigation and Water Resources statement, 15 July 2020; Reuters, 15 July 2020

sources.claim: Sudanese officials have said the dam can regulate the river and reduce floods
sources.source: Sudan Ministry of Irrigation statements, 2020; Reuters, 2020

sources.claim: Al-Fashaga is claimed by both Sudan and Ethiopia; troops have clashed there since late 2020
sources.source: Reuters and Crisis Group reporting, Dec 2020 – 2021

sources.claim: The Aswan High Dam was completed in 1970; Lake Nasser holds about 162 billion cubic metres
sources.source: Egyptian Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Aswan High Dam

sources.claim: Egypt has more than 105 million people
sources.source: CAPMAS (Egypt's statistics agency), population clock announcement, Feb 2024 (106 million)

sources.claim: 1929 exchange of notes: no upstream works that reduce Egypt's water or change its timing without Egypt's agreement
sources.source: Exchange of Notes between the United Kingdom and Egypt regarding the use of the Waters of the Nile, Cairo, 7 May 1929

sources.claim: Egypt and Ethiopia dispute the 1902 treaty's validity; Ethiopia says it was not ratified and the Amharic text differs
sources.source: Salman M. A. Salman, 'The Nile Basin Cooperative Framework Agreement', Water International, 2013; Ethiopian Ministry of Foreign Affairs statements

sources.claim: 1959 agreement: Egypt 55.5, Sudan 18.5, about 10 billion cubic metres for evaporation; Ethiopia not a party
sources.source: Agreement between Egypt and Sudan for the Full Utilization of the Nile Waters, 8 Nov 1959

sources.claim: A US Bureau of Reclamation survey published in 1964 mapped Blue Nile dam sites, including one near the Sudan border
sources.source: US Bureau of Reclamation, Land and Water Resources of the Blue Nile Basin: Ethiopia, 1964

sources.claim: No large dam on the main Blue Nile in Ethiopia before GERD
sources.source: International Rivers, GERD fact sheet; Nile Basin Initiative, 2012

sources.claim: Cooperative Framework Agreement signed in Entebbe in May 2010; based on equitable and reasonable utilization
sources.source: Agreement on the Nile River Basin Cooperative Framework, opened for signature 14 May 2010, Art. 4

sources.claim: The CFA entered into force in October 2024 after South Sudan ratified, with six parties; Egypt and Sudan reject it
sources.source: Nile Basin Initiative statement, 13 Oct 2024; Egyptian and Sudanese ministry statements, Oct 2024

sources.claim: Egypt's revolution came weeks before the April 2011 foundation stone
sources.source: Mubarak resigned 11 Feb 2011 (Reuters); foundation stone 2 April 2011

sources.claim: Ethiopia funded the dam largely itself through its budget, bonds and public contributions; reported cost about $5 billion
sources.source: Reuters, 9 Sept 2025; Office of the National Council for the Coordination of Public Participation on the GERD

sources.claim: Declaration of Principles signed in Khartoum in March 2015, pledging to avoid significant harm
sources.source: Agreement on Declaration of Principles on the GERD, Khartoum, 23 March 2015, Principle III

sources.claim: Ethiopia announced the first filling in July 2020, attributing it to rainfall; Egypt and Sudan objected
sources.source: Office of the Prime Minister of Ethiopia, 21 July 2020; Reuters, 21–22 July 2020

sources.claim: Ethiopia announced a fifth filling by September 2024
sources.source: Ethiopian government statements; Reuters, Sept 2024

sources.claim: First turbine generating in February 2022
sources.source: Reuters, 20 Feb 2022

sources.claim: Washington talks (US Treasury, World Bank) ended in February 2020; Egypt initialed a draft, Ethiopia did not attend
sources.source: US Treasury statement, 28 Feb 2020; Egyptian Foreign Ministry, 28 Feb 2020

sources.claim: In October 2020 Trump said Egypt could end up 'blowing up' the dam; Ethiopia summoned the US ambassador
sources.source: Reuters, 24 Oct 2020

sources.claim: UN Security Council met on the dam in 2020 and 2021 and encouraged AU-led talks
sources.source: UNSC meetings 29 June 2020 and 8 July 2021; Presidential Statement S/PRST/2021/18, 15 Sept 2021

sources.claim: Last formal round ended December 2023; Egypt said talks failed; Ethiopia blamed Egypt's positions
sources.source: Egyptian Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation, 19 Dec 2023; Ethiopian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 20 Dec 2023

sources.claim: Egypt's renewable water is near 550 cubic metres per person a year; below 1,000 counts as scarcity
sources.source: FAO AQUASTAT, Egypt country profile (2020); Falkenmark water stress indicator

sources.claim: Egypt seeks a binding agreement with drought releases and dispute settlement
sources.source: Egyptian Foreign Ministry letters to the UN Security Council, 2020–2021

sources.claim: Sisi: 'No one can take a drop of water from Egypt, and if it happens there will be inconceivable instability in the region'
sources.source: President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, Suez Canal remarks, 30 March 2021 (Reuters translation)

sources.claim: Ethiopia says the dam is for power, not irrigation, and water passes downstream; it prefers guidelines to a binding deal that would entrench the 1959 shares
sources.source: Ethiopian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, statements to the UN Security Council, 2020–2021

sources.claim: Ethiopia exports power to Sudan, Djibouti and Kenya
sources.source: Ethiopian Electric Power annual reports; Kenya Power, Ethiopia–Kenya interconnector, 2022

sources.claim: October 2025 floods: Egypt's water ministry blamed GERD releases; Ethiopia said the dam reduced flooding
sources.source: Egyptian Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation statement, Oct 2025; Ethiopian Ministry of Water and Energy response, Oct 2025

sources.claim: Ethiopia–Somaliland port memorandum January 2024; Egypt–Somalia defence protocol August 2024
sources.source: Reuters, 1 Jan 2024; Reuters, 14 Aug 2024

sources.claim: The Nile ran well below average from 1979 to 1987; Lake Nasser fell close to the minimum for power by 1988
sources.source: Declan Conway, 'From headwater tributaries to international river', Global Environmental Change, 2005

sources.claim: Egypt says it reserves the right to protect its water security
sources.source: Egyptian Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation, 19 Dec 2023

sources.claim: Ethiopia says it does not intend to harm its neighbours
sources.source: PM Abiy Ahmed, inauguration speech, 9 Sept 2025 (AP, Reuters)

sources.claim: Some 60 million people depend on the lower Mekong
sources.source: Mekong River Commission, State of the Basin Report, 2018
